sn22.22:1.1: This discourse is much quoted in later texts of both Pali and Sanskrit Buddhism, especially in discussing what the Buddha meant by “individual” (_puggala_). One school of Buddhism, the Pudgalavādins, argued that the “individual” was ultimately real but not defined, being neither identical with nor separate from the aggregates. This position was rejected by other schools, including the Theravada ([kv1.1]()). The text itself, however is not really about the nature of personal identity, but about spiritual responsibility.
sn22.22:1.2: “Burden” (_bhāra_) has the dual senses of “load” and “responsibility”. The opening phrase clearly indicates three of the four noble truths (the burden = suffering, picking up = origin, putting down = cessation), leaving the status of the “bearer of the burden” unclear. I propose that the sequence of the truths has been altered for rhetorical purposes, and the “bearer of the burden” is a person who has undertaken the path. Compare [an2.98]()–99, where the fool is the one who “carries the burden” (i.e. “shoulders responsibility”) for what has not come to be, but does not “carry the burden” for what is present, while the astute are the opposite.
sn22.22:1.5: Vedic _skandha_ has no technical use, being simply the “trunk” of a tree (Rig Veda 1.32.5, Atharva Veda 10.7.38) or a person (plural = “shoulders”, Atharva Veda 6.25.2, 6.135.1, etc.). The Buddhist use shares more in common with the Jains, for whom the _skandha_ was a type of matter (_pudgala_) consisting of two or more combined “atoms” (_aṇu_), namely a “molecule” (Tattvārthasūtra 5.5). Thus the aggregates themselves can be considered what “shoulders” the burden (like buffaloes, Arthaśāstra 2.29.8).
sn22.22:2.1: _Bhārahāra_ is attested almost entirely in discussion of this discourse. However, we do find an unrelated idiomatic use in the commentary to [an3.91](), where it means “one who takes responsibility” (for looking after a monastery). Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka 14.2 speaks of a student who repeats the Veda without understanding, like a pillar that merely “bears the burden” (_bhārahāra_). This is also in reference to a person who has undertaken a responsibility.
sn22.22:2.2: _Puggala_ (Sanskrit _pudgala_) is a primarily Buddhist and Jain term, being absent from pre-Buddhist texts and rare later. Pali is rich in terms for a “person” (_purisa_, _jana_, _jantu_, _nara_, _manussa_, etc.), so why did _puggala_ became so characteristic in Buddhism? It is the normal term used especially in the Aṅguttara Nikāya when describing certain “individuals” and their characteristics; these are collected in the Abhidhamma book the Puggalapaññatti. The Jain meaning of _pudgala_ is “mass”, “matter” (Tattvārthasūtra 5.5). Likewise it is used for a “mass” (of gold) by Kauṭilya (Arthaśastra 2.14.7, 2.14.43). Indeed, related to a criticism of those who believe in not-self, i.e. Buddhists, we find the notion that beings are _pudgalāśrayāḥ_ (“comprised of a composite mass”, Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.30.13). Thus _puggala_ connects with the idea of _khandha_ as an “aggregate”, “bundle”. Perhaps the Buddha favored _puggala_ because it avoided Vedic terminology, while at the same time suggesting a connection with the _khandha_ doctrine that the “person” comprised a “mass” of components. Try reading this Sutta and substituting “mass” for “individual”.
sn22.22:2.3: The commentary says this refers to any person from the time of birth, and this understanding is shared in the Buddhist tradition generally. However, it does not explain why, if the individual means any person, they referred to as “venerable”. I think this implies that they are a spiritual practitioner who has “undertaken responsibility” for the path of practice, thus standing in for the otherwise-missing fourth noble truth.
